texts.exact_text: Kî Žî intimates progress and success in small matters. There will be advantage in being firm and correct. There has been good fortune in the beginning; there may be disorder in the end.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, hexagram statement
texts.notes: Legge's title restored from the source statement.

texts.exact_text: The first NINE, undivided, (shows its subject as a driver) who drags back his wheel, (or as a fox) which has wet his tail. There will be no error.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, line 1

texts.exact_text: The second SIX, divided, (shows its subject as) a wife who has lost her (carriage-)screen. There is no occasion to go in pursuit of it. In seven days she will find it.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, line 2

texts.exact_text: The third NINE, undivided, (suggests the case of) Gāo Zōng, who attacked the Demon region, but was three years in subduing it. Small men should not be employed (in such enterprises).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, line 3

texts.exact_text: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject with rags provided against any leak (in his boat), and on his guard all day long.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, line 4

texts.exact_text: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject (as) the neighbour in the east who slaughters an ox (for his sacrifice); but this is not equal to the (small) spring sacrifice of the neighbour in the west, whose sincerity receives the blessing.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, line 5

texts.exact_text: The topmost SIX, divided, shows its subject with (even) his head immersed. The position is perilous.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, line 6

texts.exact_text:
The character called jì(既) is used as a symbol of being past or completed. Jì(济) denotes primarily crossing a stream, and has the secondary meaning of helping and completing. The two characters, combined, will express the successful accomplishment of whatever the writer has in his mind. In dealing with this lineal figure, king Wén was thinking of the condition of the kingdom, at length at rest and quiet. The vessel of the state has been brought safely across the great and dangerous stream. The distresses of the kingdom have been relieved, and its disorders have been repressed. Does anything remain to be done still? Yes, in small things. The new government has to be consolidated. Its ruler must, without noise or clamour, go on to perfect what has been wrought, with firmness and correctness, and ever keeping in mind the instability of all human affairs. That every line of the hexagram is in its correct place, and has its proper correlate is also supposed to harmonize with the intimation of progress and success.

Line 1, the first of the hexagram, represents the time immediately after the successful achievement of the enterprise it denotes; -- the time for resting and being quiet. For a season, at least, all movement should be hushed. Hence we have the symbolism of a driver trying to stop his carriage, and a fox who has wet his tail, and will not tempt the stream again.

Line 2 is weak, and in its proper place. It also has the strong correlate 5; and might be expected to be forward to act. But it occupies its correct and central place, and suggests the symbol of a lady whose carriage has lost its screen. She will not advance further so soon after success has been achieved; but keep herself hidden and retired. Let her not try to find the screen. When it is said that she will find this after seven days, the meaning seems to be simply this, that the period of Kî Žî will then have been exhausted, the six lines having been gone through, and a new period, when action will be proper, shall have commenced.

The strong line 3, at the top of the lower trigram ☲, suggests for its subject one undertaking a vigorous enterprise. The writer thinks of Gāo Zōng, the sacrificial title of Wǔ Dīng, one of the ablest sovereigns of the Shāng dynasty (B. C. 1364 - 1324), who undertook an expedition against the barbarous hordes of the cold and bleak regions north of the Middle States. He is mentioned again under the next hexagram. He appears also in the Shū Jīng, IV, ix, and in the Shī Jīng, IV, iii, ode 5. His enterprise may have been good, and successful, but it was tedious, and the paragraph concludes with a caution.

Line 4 is weak, and has advanced into the trigram ☵ for water. Its subject will be cautious, and prepare for evil, as in the symbolism, suggested probably by the nature of the trigram ☵.

The neighbour in the East is the subject of line 5, and the neighbour in the West is the subject of the correlate 2, the former quarter being yáng and the latter yīn. Line 5 is strong, and 2 is weak; but weakness is more likely to be patient and cautious than strength. They are compared to two men sacrificing. The one presents valuable offerings; the other very poor ones. But the second excels in sincerity, and his small offering is the more acceptable.

The topmost line is weak, and on the outmost edge of ☵ Kǎn, the trigram, of peril. His action is violent and perilous, like that one attempting to cross a ford, and being plunged overhead into the water. 既济 ䷾
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Hexagram 63; scan-backed transcription p. 204, notes

texts.exact_text: 既濟：亨小。利貞。初吉終亂。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 易經卦辭

texts.exact_text: 既濟，亨，小者亨也。利貞，剛柔正而位當也。初吉，柔得中也。終止則亂，其道窮也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 彖

texts.exact_text: 水在火上，既濟；君子以思患而豫防之。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 大象

texts.exact_text: 初九：曳其輪，濡其尾，无咎。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 爻 1

texts.exact_text: 曳其輪，義无咎也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 小象 1

texts.exact_text: 六二：婦喪其茀，勿逐，七日得。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 爻 2

texts.exact_text: 七日得，以中道也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 小象 2

texts.exact_text: 九三：高宗伐鬼方，三年克之，小人勿用。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 爻 3

texts.exact_text: 三年克之，憊也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 小象 3

texts.exact_text: 六四：繻有衣袽，終日戒。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 爻 4

texts.exact_text: 終日戒，有所疑也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 小象 4

texts.exact_text: 九五：東鄰殺牛，不如西鄰之禴祭，實受其福。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 爻 5

texts.exact_text: 東鄰殺牛，不如西鄰之時也；實受其福，吉大來也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 小象 5

texts.exact_text: 上六：濡其首，厲。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 爻 6

texts.exact_text: 濡其首厲，何可久也。
texts.locator: Chinese Wikisource 周易/既濟; cross-checked against CTP Book of Changes, hexagram 63, 小象 6

texts.exact_text:
'Kî Žî intimates progress and success:' -- in small matters, that is, there will be that progress and success.

'There will be advantage in being firm and correct:' -- the strong and weak (lines) are correctly arranged, each in its appropriate place.

'There has been good fortune in the beginning:' -- the weak (second line) is in the centre.

In the end there is a cessation (of effort), and disorder arises: -- the course (that led to rule and order) is (now) exhausted.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix I, Hexagram 63, p. unpaginated transcription

texts.exact_text: (The trigram ☲ representing) fire and ☵ that for water above it form Kî Žî. The superior man, in accordance with this, thinks of evil (that may come), and beforehand guards against it.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 63, p. 346

texts.exact_text: 'He drags back his wheel:' -- as we may rightly judge, there will be no mistake.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 63, line 1, p. 346

texts.exact_text: 'In seven days she will find it:' -- for the course pursued is that indicated by the central position (of the line).
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 63, line 2, p. 346

texts.exact_text: 'He was three years in subduing it:' -- enough to make him weary.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 63, line 3, p. 346

texts.exact_text: 'He is on his guard all the day:' -- he is in doubt about something.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 63, line 4, p. 346

texts.exact_text: 'The slaughtering of an ox by the neighbour in the east is not equal to (the small sacrifice of) the neighbour in the west:' -- because the time (in the latter case is more important and fit). 'His sincerity receives the blessing:' -- good fortune comes on a great scale.
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 63, line 5, p. 346

texts.exact_text: 'His head is immersed; the position is perilous:' -- how could such a state continue long?
texts.locator: SBE XVI, Appendix II, Hexagram 63, line 6, p. 346
